title: Interfaces
summary: An interface names the information an object should contain.

subtopics.title: Properties
subtopics.explanation: A property lists a name and its expected type, such as `id: number`. It is like a labeled field on a form. TypeScript checks that code using the interface supplies compatible values, helping catch mistakes before the program runs. For example, a `Product` interface can require a numeric ID and a string title. For example, require an ID while allowing a display name to be absent.

subtopics.title: Optional fields
subtopics.explanation: A question mark makes a property optional, such as `nickname?: string`. The property may be absent, so code must check before using it. It is like a form question that can be left blank. Optional does not automatically mean the value can be `null`. For example, a nickname can be optional while a user ID stays required. For example, use a shared interface for the props accepted by several related components.

subtopics.title: Extend a shape
subtopics.explanation: An interface can extend another interface to add fields while keeping the original properties. It is like building a specialized form from a standard one. Use extension when the types share a real relationship; avoid long chains that make the final shape hard to discover. For example, a premium account shape can extend a basic account with a plan field. For example, extend an interface when a specialized object truly includes the base fields.

subtopics.title: Shape checking
subtopics.explanation: TypeScript usually checks objects by their shape, not by their class name. An object with the required compatible properties can satisfy an interface. It is like accepting a form because its fields are present. This structural approach makes small data objects easy to pass between functions. For example, a plain object can satisfy an interface even when it was not created by a class. For example, a plain object can match a type without being an instance of a class.

subtopics.title: Outside data
subtopics.explanation: An interface helps during development but does not validate network data at runtime. Type annotations are removed when JavaScript runs. It is like printing a checklist without inspecting the delivered package. Validate external values and then use the interface to describe the checked result. For example, parse and validate server JSON before assigning it the interface type. For example, validate a network object before asserting that it satisfies the interface.

foundations.overview: An interface describes the properties an object should have. TypeScript compares objects with that shape while checking code. Think of it like a shared form template that lists required fields. Interfaces help during development but disappear at runtime, so validate values received from a server or user before trusting them.
foundations.whyItMatters: Interfaces make object expectations visible and reusable. They improve compile-time feedback, but runtime values still need validation at the boundary.
foundations.browserPerspective: Interfaces exist only at compile time and are completely erased — the emitted JavaScript contains no interfaces and no runtime shape checks. They influence what the compiler allows you to write, not what runs in the browser.
foundations.realWorldUsage: React component props (interface Props), API response shapes, function option bags ({ retries?: number }), and class contracts (implements Repository) are all expressed as interfaces in everyday TypeScript code.
foundations.businessImpact: Well-defined interfaces act as enforced contracts between teams and modules, so a change to a data shape surfaces as compile errors at every consumer rather than as runtime bugs in production.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Interfaces enable programming to a contract: code depends on a shape, not a concrete implementation, which makes substitution, mocking in tests, and refactoring safe and mechanical.
foundations.performanceImpact: Zero runtime cost — interfaces are erased. As a bonus, the compiler can often type-check against named interfaces faster and produce clearer error messages than against large inline object types.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Interfaces exist at runtime and validate objects.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Interfaces are erased at compile time; they perform no runtime checks. To validate data at runtime you need an explicit check or a validation library.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An object must be declared as the interface type to satisfy it.
commonMisconceptions.reality: TypeScript is structural — any object with a compatible shape satisfies the interface, regardless of how or where it was created.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An interface creates a JavaScript object at runtime.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Interfaces are removed from emitted JavaScript; they describe expectations during checking.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An interface makes server data trustworthy.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Runtime validation is needed because incoming values may not follow the declared shape.

visualExplorer.title: How an interface contract is checked
visualExplorer.caption: Step through declaring an interface and assigning objects to it, watching the compiler enforce the shape.

config.intro: Trace how interface User { id: number; name: string } is enforced.

steps.name: Declare the interface
steps.detail: interface User { id: number; name: string } names a contract: every User needs a numeric id and a string name.

steps.name: Annotate a variable
steps.detail: const u: User = ... tells the compiler u must satisfy the User shape.

steps.name: Check required members
steps.detail: The compiler verifies id and name are present with the correct types — a missing field is an error.

steps.name: Reject extra/wrong fields
steps.detail: An object literal with a typo'd or mistyped property fails the check at compile time.

steps.name: Extend the contract
steps.detail: interface Admin extends User adds members while inheriting id and name.

steps.name: Erase at compile time
steps.detail: The interface vanishes from the output; only the plain JavaScript object remains at runtime.

interactiveExamples.title: Defining and using an interface
interactiveExamples.explanation: The interface names the shape; objects assigned to it must match. Optional and readonly modifiers refine the contract.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Ada Lovelace / no nickname / id stays 1

interactiveExamples.title: Extending and implementing
interactiveExamples.explanation: Admin inherits User's members via extends, and a class implements the contract so the compiler enforces conformance.

codeLab.title: Define a Product interface
codeLab.instructions: Create an interface Product with a readonly id (number), a name (string), a price (number), and an optional discount (number). Then write describe(p: Product) returning a string. Use the discount when present.
hints: Use readonly for id and ? for the optional discount.
Annotate describe's parameter as Product and its return as string.

keyTakeaways: A property lists a name and its expected type, such as `id: number`.
A question mark makes a property optional, such as `nickname?: string`.
An interface can extend another interface to add fields while keeping the original properties.
TypeScript usually checks objects by their shape, not by their class name.
An interface helps during development but does not validate network data at runtime.
